# The shape of a Qt Quick application {#sec-shape}

Before getting into details, let's look at the big picture: which code goes where, and how
the parts talk to each other. Every later chapter fills in one part of this picture.

## QML composes, C++ implements {#sec-split}

Qt Quick splits an application by language. C++ holds the state and the logic and offers
them as properties, signals and methods. QML arranges the visual components and wires their
properties to that state.

```{.cpp filename="CanvasStore.hpp"}
class CanvasStore : public QObject
{
    Q_OBJECT
    QML_ELEMENT
    Q_PROPERTY(bool canUndo READ canUndo NOTIFY changed FINAL)

public:
    bool canUndo() const;
    Q_INVOKABLE void undo();

Q_SIGNALS:
    void changed();
};
```

```{.qml filename="CanvasPage.qml"}
ToolButton {
    text: qsTr("Undo")
    enabled: store.canUndo   // a binding: follows the store's state by itself
    onClicked: store.undo()  // a handler: sends the user's intent to C++
}
```

Moving that button, restyling it or putting it in a menu is a QML change that touches no
logic. In Qt Widgets, layout and logic both live in C++, so the same change means editing
and recompiling code. The split by language is also a split by responsibility, and that is
the main reason to choose Qt Quick.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/canvas/CanvasStore.hpp`, `src/canvas/CanvasPage.qml`

**Read more:** [Qt Quick best practices](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtquick-bestpractices.html)
:::

## Layers, with Qt's names {#sec-layers}

Most Qt Quick applications settle into four layers. Qt projects name them differently from
textbooks, so here are both:

| Layer | Name in Qt projects | Holds | Template example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Presentation | **View** | QML: layout, input, animation | `SketchbookPage.qml` |
| Application | **ViewModel** or **Controller** | QObjects that turn user intent into operations | `SketchbookViewModel` |
| Domain | **Core** or **Engine** | Plain C++ rules and algorithms | `shapes::Recognizer` |
| Infrastructure | **Backend**, **Storage**, **Network** | Files, sockets, devices | `SketchStorage` |

Only the view is QML. Only the view model knows that QML exists. The core knows about
neither of them, which is why it is the easiest code to test and to reuse.

## Commands go down, notifications come up {#sec-flow}

A layer calls the layer below it directly. The lower layer never calls back up; it emits a
signal, and whoever cares listens. In QML, listening happens through bindings.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant V as View (QML)
    participant VM as ViewModel (C++)
    participant S as Storage (C++)
    V->>VM: rename(row, "Floor plan")
    VM->>S: save(id, document)
    VM-->>V: dataChanged (signal)
    Note over V: bindings update the row
```

Because lower layers never know who listens, you can test them without a UI and replace the
UI without touching them.

## Dependencies point one way, and the build enforces it {#sec-direction}

Each layer and feature may only use what sits below it. Write that rule into the build: a
library can only include headers of the libraries it links.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A[app] --> SB[sketchbook] --> C[canvas] --> SH[shapes]
    SB --> ST[style]
    C --> ST
```

```{.cmake filename="CMakeLists.txt"}
target_link_libraries(app_canvas PUBLIC shapes::shapes)
target_link_libraries(app_sketchbook PUBLIC app_canvas)
```

When `canvas` tries to include a `sketchbook` header, the compiler refuses. A broken rule
fails the build on the spot, long before a code review would catch it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Lower layers never know their callers
A lower layer never includes, links or calls anything above it; when it has news, it emits
a signal (@sec-flow). If code only works with an upward include, it sits in the wrong layer:
move it down, or pass the dependency in from `main()`.
:::

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/CMakeLists.txt` and the `CMakeLists.txt` of each feature
:::

## One place wires everything {#sec-composition-root}

Some code has to know every concrete type and connect them. Keep that code in one place,
`main()`, and nowhere else. It creates the long-lived objects, gives each one its dependencies,
and passes them to QML.

```{.cpp filename="main.cpp"}
int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
    QGuiApplication application(argc, argv);

    SketchStorage storage(dataDir);              // <1>
    CanvasStore canvas;
    SketchbookViewModel sketchbook(storage, canvas);

    QQmlApplicationEngine engine;                // <2>
    engine.setInitialProperties({
        { "sketchbook", QVariant::fromValue(&sketchbook) },
        { "canvas", QVariant::fromValue(&canvas) },
    });
    engine.loadFromModule("App", "Main");
    return application.exec();
}
```
1. Objects receive their dependencies through the constructor. No globals.
2. The engine is created last and destroyed first, so QML never sees an object that is already gone.

Every lifetime is visible in one function, and a test can build the same objects with simple
stand-ins for the real ones.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/app/main.cpp`
:::

## Interfaces at the seams {#sec-interfaces}

Where your code meets the outside world (a network, a device, the clock), put an abstract
class between them. The rest of the app depends on the interface, so a test can pass in a
simple version of its own.

```{.cpp filename="Transport.hpp"}
class Transport
{
public:
    virtual ~Transport() = default;
    virtual void send(const QByteArray &payload) = 0;
};

class TcpTransport final : public Transport { /* the real network */ };
class RecordingTransport final : public Transport { /* records what was sent, for tests */ };
```

Name the interface after what it is, `Transport`, and each implementation after how it
works: `TcpTransport`, `RecordingTransport`. Callers only ever see `Transport` and never
need to know whether it is abstract. Qt follows this rule for its own I/O: `QIODevice` is
the
abstract base of `QFile` and `QTcpSocket`.

In real code you will meet two other conventions:

- **An `Abstract` prefix**, as in `QAbstractItemModel` or `QAbstractButton`. Qt uses it for
  base classes that already implement most of the behavior and are meant for you to
  subclass.
- **An `I` prefix**, as in `ITransport`. It comes from COM and C#, where every interface
  carries it, and is common in C++ code that grew up on Windows.

Each is fine where it is the house style. When you extend a framework, follow its
convention; in your own code, start with the plain noun and stay consistent.

Add an interface only once a second implementation exists, even if only a test uses it.
Before that, it is indirection with nothing behind it. The template's storage has no
interface: its tests write to a temporary folder instead.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [C++ Core Guidelines, NL.5](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#rl-name-type)
:::
